notes:
I've written the notes below verse by verse. Not everything you asked for is here, so here are the gaps first:

- **What I read:** Enduring Word (David Guzik, a Calvary Chapel pastor), Ellicott's notes up to v. 18 (the page cut off there), BibleHub's verse-commentary pages for vv. 1, 2, 13 and 26, and a few topical articles.
- **What's missing:** I didn't reach Gill or the Pulpit Commentary as full chapters, preceptaustin's page on this chapter, or any Lutheran, Methodist, Catholic, Orthodox or modern-scholarship pages.
- **Thin spots:** vv. 19–25 and 27 have little verse-level detail.
- **Who disagrees:** The sources I read don't show Protestant traditions splitting along denominational lines anywhere in this chapter. The real disagreements are: whether the Amalekite was lying; whether David believed him; how to read v. 26; and how "the LORD's anointed" (v. 14) applies to pastors today.

**v. 1**
- Ellicott says this verse picks up straight from 1 Samuel 31 and 30. The two books really form one continuous narrative. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/1.htm
- Ellicott places Ziklag about four days' journey from Mount Gilboa. and the messenger who brought the news of the battle must have left the field before David's return to Ziklag. (same URL)
- Keil & Delitzsch say we can't tell whether the battle happened before or after David got back. All the verse shows is that the two events happened at about the same time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/1-1.htm
- Guzik notes that David had earlier sided with the Philistines out of despair. God brought him back through the Amalekite raid on Ziklag. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-1/

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: "the third day" means three days after David's return, not after Saul's death. Bowing down was more than politeness; it treated David as the new king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/1.htm
- Guzik: torn clothes and dust were the usual signs of mourning, so David knew at once the news was bad. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-1/
- One note on BibleHub's v. 2 page rejects the old idea that the messenger was Doeg the Edomite. Another commentator there thinks he was not a soldier but one of the hangers-on who follow armies looking for loot. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/1-2.htm

**v. 3**
- Ellicott: he clearly claims to have been part of Israel's camp. His summary of the defeat and the two deaths is accurate. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/1.htm

**vv. 4–5** — Guzik: on hearing the news, David asks how the man knows. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-1/

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: the Israelites probably broke and ran up Gilboa, and the Amalekite came across Saul during that scattered retreat. Ellicott calls it extremely unlikely that he found him without warriors or armour-bearer, wounded and alone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/1.htm
- Guzik also doubts the story. He quotes Adam Clarke calling it made up, and notes that 1 Samuel 31:5 says the armor-bearer saw that Saul was already dead. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-1/
- Constable agrees the account was probably inaccurate, given 1 Samuel 31 and 1 Chronicles 10. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-1.html

**v. 8**
- Ellicott sketches Amalek's history as Israel's long-time enemy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/1.htm
- Guzik: if the story is true, it is chilling that an Amalekite finished off Saul, who had failed to destroy Amalek. He says Amalek is "commonly regarded" as a picture of our sinful nature, while admitting the Bible doesn't say so. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-1/
- Clarke quotes Dr. Delaney: an Amalekite took that crown from off the head of Saul, which he had forfeited by his disobedience in the case of Amalek. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-samuel-1.html

**v. 9** — Ellicott: the word translated "agony/anguish" appears only here. The rabbis took it as cramp, others as dizziness. It probably means some effect of Saul's wound that left him unable to fight. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/1.htm

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: the story contradicts 1 Samuel 31:4–5 and was made up to win David's favour. Still, the man must have been among the first to reach Saul's body, since he had the crown and armband. Handing them over shows he saw David as the coming king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/1.htm
- Matthew Henry thinks Saul was vain enough to wear these ornaments into battle, which made him an easy target for archers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_001.cfm

**vv. 11–12**
- Ellicott sees no reason to doubt David's grief was real. It was grief for the king, for Jonathan, for God's people, and for his country. He notes the one deep mourning for Saul came from the man Saul had hunted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/1.htm
- Guzik: bitterness and unforgiveness are things we choose. David chose to become "better, not bitter," and his men followed him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-1/
- Henry: instead of the delight the Amalekite expected, David wept and fasted, even for Saul his enemy. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_001.cfm

**v. 13**
- Ellicott: the question is now asked formally, as in a trial. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/1-13.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: "son of a foreigner" means the son of an Amalekite who had settled in Israel. (same URL)

**v. 14**
- Ellicott: whether or not David believed the story, the man had to be judged on his own word. To David, killing the king was a grave religious offence, as his own refusals to kill Saul showed (1 Samuel 24 and 26). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/1.htm
- Guzik: God put Saul on the throne, so ending his reign was God's job. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-1/
- Constable says the opposite of Ellicott on one point: David had him executed because he believed his story. Constable also notes that all but one of the eleven uses of "the LORD's anointed" are in 1–2 Samuel. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-1.html
- **Debated modern use (leaders immune from criticism):**
  - GotQuestions says the "touch not God's anointed" verses are sometimes used in Pentecostal and Charismatic circles to defend certain preachers from criticism. It answers that all believers are anointed. https://www.gotquestions.org/touch-not-Gods-anointed.html
  - A Ligonier devotional calls it the reply of those who do not have an argument or an example to give as an answer. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/do-not-touch-the-lords-anointed
  - Conrad Mbewe (TGC Africa) argues it is about physical harm, not fair criticism. Otherwise Samuel and Nathan were wrong to rebuke kings. https://africa.thegospelcoalition.org/article/touch-not-the-lords-anointed/
  - Grace to You (John MacArthur's ministry) criticizes Benny Hinn for using it against his critics. https://www.gty.org/blogs/B170410/did-god-forbid-us-to-critique-or-criticize-church-leaders

**vv. 15–16**
- Ellicott: by bowing to David, the man had accepted his authority. And by his own confession he was guilty of high treason. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/1.htm
- Guzik: the execution shows David's grief was real. Even with excuses (Saul asked; he was dying anyway), only God may end a life outside war, self-defence or lawful punishment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-1/
- Henry: the man's pleas were overruled, and David was not unjust. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_001.cfm

**v. 17**
- Ellicott: "lament" is the technical term for a funeral song, like David's for Abner. This is almost the only non-religious poem of David's we have. He quotes Keil praising it as one of the finest odes in the Old Testament. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/1.htm

**v. 18**
- Ellicott: the KJV's "the use of [the bow]" isn't in the Hebrew. "The Bow" is the song's title. (same URL)
- Guzik: the Book of Jashar, also mentioned in Joshua 10:13, was a collection of early Hebrew poetry. It is not a "lost" book of the Bible. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-1/

**vv. 19–25**
- Guzik: David saw beauty in Saul and wanted no one to gloat. He called even the mountains, and Israel's women, to mourn, praising Saul's courage and loyalty. This shows a heart free of bitterness (1 Corinthians 13:5; 1 Peter 4:8). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-1/
- Guzik on "how the mighty have fallen": Saul really fell much earlier, when he hardened his heart against God. (same URL)
- Constable: David began his kingship as a shepherd rather than a warrior. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-1.html

**v. 26 (the most debated verse)**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Ellicott compares Jonathan's love to a faithful wife's, an affection such as could only exist between noble natures and those united in the fear of God. https://biblehub.com/2_samuel/1-26.htm
  - Gill gives the Targum and the rabbi Kimchi: "more than the love of two women," meaning David's wives Ahinoam and Abigail. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/1-26.htm
  - Keil & Delitzsch: comparing it to a woman's love expresses the deepest devoted love. (same URL)
  - Henry: Jonathan was loyal to the rival who would take his crown. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/1-26.html
- **Spurgeon (Baptist)** reads Jonathan's love as a small picture of Christ's love. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/the-love-of-jonathan-and-the-love-of-jesus/
- **Guzik** adds that David's experience of love with women was not as God intended. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-1/
- **Sexual reading, rejected:**
  - Constable says the word for "love" here is used for "friendship" in Psalm 109, and here means covenant and political loyalty. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/1-26.html
  - GotQuestions gives three reasons, one being that David may be contrasting Jonathan with Saul's daughters, who were offered to him with conditions. https://www.gotquestions.org/David-and-Jonathan.html
  - Guzik rejects the "progressive" reading in a separate Q&A. https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/qa-transcripts/david-jonathan-gay/
- **Catholic translation:** the Douay-Rheims has an extra line, "As the mother loveth her only son, so did I love thee." So does Wycliffe. I found no Catholic commentary explaining it. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/2-samuel/1-26.html

**v. 27** — I didn't find verse-level notes beyond Guzik's general remarks above.
